title: Round 9: Design a migration from monolith to modular architecture
description: Plan a step-by-step migration from a monolithic application to a modular or service-oriented architecture without disrupting customers.

data.text: The interviewer asks you to move a mature product from a single deployable unit to independently deployable modules. The challenge is not just technical: it is about minimizing risk, preserving feature velocity, and convincing stakeholders that the migration is worth the investment.

rows: Split by business capability such as billing or inventory
Complex domains with clear bounded contexts
Move infrastructure or shared libraries first, then features
Reducing compile times and team ownership
May not deliver customer value quickly
Route new features to new services, gradually replacing the monolith
Requires a proxy layer and careful routing

terms.definition: An anti-corruption layer that gradually replaces a legacy system by intercepting requests and routing them to new services.
Multiple services that are so tightly coupled that they must be deployed together, defeating the purpose of microservices.
A boundary within a domain where a particular model is defined and applicable, used to guide service decomposition.
A translation layer that protects the new system from the legacy system's model and vice versa.

data.text: Domain-driven decomposition is usually the most durable because it aligns services with business capabilities. Layered extraction is faster to start but can leave you with a distributed monolith. The strangler fig pattern is excellent for high-availability systems because the old system keeps running while the new one absorbs traffic.

data.title: Strangler fig in practice
data.content: An API gateway or reverse proxy inspects the request path and routes it:
data.code:
Request path /api/v2/orders  → New Orders Service
Request path /api/v1/orders  → Legacy Monolith

Over time:
- /v1 endpoints shrink as features move to /v2
- The monolith handles only legacy customers
- Eventually the monolith is retired

data.text: A migration is a team change as much as a technical change. If you extract Notifications into a service but the same team still owns both, you have added operational overhead without gaining autonomy. Align service boundaries with team boundaries using Conway's Law.

items: Map each module to a team before extracting it.
Give each team full ownership: code, deployments, on-call, and SLAs.
Create a platform team to provide shared infrastructure (CI/CD, observability, secrets).
Document the migration roadmap with clear milestones and exit criteria.
Celebrate each extraction as a team victory, not just a technical milestone.
Extract data ownership first: each module must own its tables or schemas.
Use asynchronous communication between modules to reduce coupling.
Run the monolith and the new module in parallel with feature flags so you can compare behavior.
Invest in observability before the migration: you need to see traffic patterns across both systems.
Plan for the end state: what does the architecture look like after the monolith is gone?
Use change-data-capture to sync monolith data to the new module in near-real time.
Run both systems in parallel and compare outputs before switching traffic.
Use feature flags to route individual customers or tenants to the new module.
Keep the old data schema writable until the new module is proven stable.
Archive or delete old data only after the migration is complete and audited.

data.caption: Strangler fig migration pattern showing gradual traffic shift from monolith to new services
data.definition:
graph LR
    A[Client] --> B[API Gateway]
    B --> C{Path matches /api/v2?}
    C -->|Yes| D[New Service]
    C -->|No| E[Legacy Monolith]
    D --> F[New Database]
    E --> G[Legacy Database]
    F --> H[Metrics: latency, errors]
    G --> H
    H --> I{Stable?}
    I -->|Yes| J[Shift more traffic]
    I -->|No| K[Rollback to monolith]
    J --> B

data.title: Keep the monolith running
data.text: The biggest mistake is trying to rewrite the monolith in secret and then flip a switch. Users do not care about your architecture; they care about uptime and features. Migrate incrementally, release often, and measure the impact on latency and error rate after every step.

cards.title: Feature flags
cards.description: Toggle new code paths at runtime without redeploying.
cons: Flag debt if not cleaned up

cards.title: Parallel run
cards.description: Run the old and new systems simultaneously and compare results.

cards.title: Canary deployment
cards.description: Roll out to a small percentage of traffic first.

items.question: How do I decide which module to extract first?
items.answer: Start with the module that has the clearest domain boundary and the lowest coupling to the rest of the monolith. Billing and notifications are common first extractions because they are often self-contained.

items.question: What if the team needs a feature before the migration is complete?
items.answer: Build the feature in the monolith first, then extract it. Do not let the migration block customer value. Use the strangler fig to route new requests to the new service once it is ready.

items.question: How do I handle shared database tables?
items.answer: Avoid shared tables between the monolith and the new module. Use APIs or events to keep data in sync. If you must share, treat it as a temporary bridge and plan to eliminate it.

items.question: What metrics should I track during the migration?
items.answer: Track request latency, error rate, data consistency checks, deployment frequency, and lead time for changes. Compare these metrics between the monolith and the new module.

data.title: Summary
points: Pick a decomposition strategy that matches your domain complexity
Extract data ownership before extracting code
Use feature flags and parallel runs to reduce risk
Invest in observability and documentation early
data.takeaway: Migration is a product decision, not just an engineering decision. Tie every step to reduced risk, faster delivery, or better reliability so stakeholders understand the value.
